title: Rajnath Singh Says Kharge's 'Baap' Remark Is an Insult to India Itself
excerpt: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh condemned Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge's ‘Modi ka baap bhi jayega’ remark in Patna as an attack on the dignity of Indian politics, as the BJP protested nationwide and the Congress defended Kharge, saying ‘baap’ meant the RSS as Modi's ideological father.
body:
• Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Monday condemned Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge's ‘Modi ka baap bhi jayega’ remark in Patna, calling it an insult to India itself and an attack on the dignity of politics.
  • Kharge made the remark on Sunday at an event marking the 139th birth anniversary of Bihar's first Chief Minister, Shri Krishna Singh, after a heckler said Prime Minister Narendra Modi would not leave power.
  • The BJP has held protests, demanded an apology, and a complaint has been filed against Kharge at Patna's Kotwali police station.
  • The Congress has defended Kharge: Pawan Khera said ‘baap’ referred to the RSS as Modi's ideological father, and other leaders called the phrase a figure of speech in response to heckling.

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Monday strongly criticised Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge over his ‘baap’ remark against Prime Minister Narendra Modi, calling it an insult to India itself and an attack on the dignity of Indian politics. Singh said the remark, made in Patna a day earlier, had left him ‘shocked and deeply hurt’, and accused the Congress of defending the statement instead of expressing regret, according to IANS.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=M0gu2Dt4ATA

‘I believe this is not just an insult to an individual or a family, but an attack on the dignity of Indian politics itself.’

— Rajnath Singh, Defence Minister

‘In a democracy, oppose as much as you like, question policies, and criticise the government, but at least do not cross the boundaries of personal decorum,’ Singh said. He added that turning ideological opposition into personal insults reflected the Congress's ‘frustration and ideological bankruptcy’, that the party had suffered ‘not just a political downfall, but a complete ideological collapse’, and that Prime Minister Modi could ‘neither be shaken by such remarks, nor can his resolve for public service be weakened’.

What Kharge said in Patna

The controversy erupted on Sunday during Kharge's address at the 139th birth anniversary celebrations of Bihar's first Chief Minister, Dr Shri Krishna Singh, in Patna. While the Congress president was criticising the Prime Minister, a person in the audience reportedly interrupted, saying Modi would not go anywhere. Kharge responded, ‘Modi ka baap bhi jayega’ — ‘Even Modi's father will have to go’ — repeating the remark, according to multiple reports of the event.

Singh stressed that the identity of the speaker was what made the episode serious: the remark ‘was not made by an ordinary Congress worker or a young leader’ but by the national president of the country's oldest political party, a position that ‘demanded greater seriousness and restraint’. He also accused Congress leaders of previously mocking the Prime Minister's family background and using objectionable language against his mother.

BJP escalates: protests and a police complaint

Rajnath Singh was not alone. Home Minister Amit Shah said Kharge had torn apart all norms of decorum, BJP president Nitin Nabin called the language ideological bankruptcy, Union Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan asked the Congress to answer for the remark or remove Kharge, and Bihar leaders demanded apologies from both Kharge and Rahul Gandhi, according to reports of the BJP's response. The BJP's Patna Metropolitan unit held a protest march on Monday, the party announced demonstrations at state headquarters across the country, and a complaint was filed against Kharge at Patna's Kotwali police station. In Bengaluru, Karnataka BJP leaders led by R. Ashoka protested at Freedom Park, and Union Minister H. D. Kumaraswamy demanded a public apology.

The Congress defence

The Congress has refused to apologise and has defended its president. Congress MP Pawan Khera said Kharge was referring to the Prime Minister's ‘ideological mentor’ — the RSS and Mohan Bhagwat — not his late father, and described the heckling of a senior leader as despicable; in Khera's account, the heckler had said Modi would not leave ‘even if your father comes’. Former Chhattisgarh Chief Minister Bhupesh Baghel called the remark a mere figure of speech and no insult, and accused the Prime Minister of using harsher language himself. Karnataka Minister Priyank Kharge, the Congress president's son, accused the BJP of turning a non-issue into a controversy and cited past BJP remarks against Congress figures. Congress MP Imran Masood said the remark was ‘absolutely justified’ and that the BJP would be answered ‘in the same language’.

What happens next

There was no word from Kharge himself on the controversy at the time of the initial reports, and the BJP shows no sign of letting the issue drop: nationwide protests, a police complaint, and a coordinated line from its senior-most ministers give the party a campaign-ready grievance, while the Congress's refusal to express regret sets up a prolonged standoff. Singh's closing warning framed the BJP's electoral pitch plainly — in a democracy, he said, ‘the public keeps track of everything, and when the time comes, they give a fitting reply’.
